author_response_spans.text: ## **RESPONSE TO REVIEWER COMMENTS**
## Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):

In this work, Perez et al. have performed detailed kinetic studies of acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX) from C. elegans in the wild-type and ATP-binding site mutants. Based on these data, they propose that ATP plays a role in enhancing the binding affinity of the FAD cofactor. To further support their model and identify how ATP can bind/relase, they performed a series of MD simulations which showed substantial fluctuations of the FAD and ATP binding sites. These fluctuations occurred in particular in an asymmetric manner between the two ACOX subunits, depending on the occupancy of the binding sites. Overall, this work presents some level of evidence suggesting that ATP allosterically regulates FAD binding, and is worth publishing after addressing the following suggestions:
## Major:

1. The reviewer is concerned about the k_cat values of the control, for example, shown in Figure 2. In both Figures 2a and 2b, I assume that the zero-time point values must be equivalent, but they range between 1.1 ~ 1.5 sec^-1. In addition, the k_cat for the control decreases over time, which the authors attribute to the unbinding of FAD and ATP. TTo clarity this, the authors should quantify the concentration of bound FAD and ATP at time zero in all experiments and consider normalizing the data in some ways based on FAD/ATP occupancy. The large variation in k_cat for the control raises the questions about the interpretation of other conditions, such as with supplied FAD and FAD/ATP.

**The initial (time zero)** _**k**_ **cat values do not coincide in Figure 2a, while they do coincide in Figure 2b, due to differences in the way the two experiments were set up.  In Figure 2a, ATP/FAD were added during the incubation, whereas in Figure 2b, the ATP/FAD were added just prior to the measurement. Thus, in Figure 2a, at time zero, the ACOX in the FAD/ATP sample was exposed to FAD/ATP for a short time period (approximately 0.5-1 min) before the measurement.  Meanwhile, in Figure 2b, the ACOX in the FAD/ATP sample had not yet been exposed to FAD/ATP at time zero.  We have clarified the differences between the time zero measurements for Figure 2a and 2b in the figure legend.**

**The** _**k**_ **cat values do not vary significantly between the different panels of Figure 2.  The** _**k**_ **cat of the control bar in Figure 2c-e corresponds to the 60 min incubation time point in Figure 2a.  Although Figure 2c-e were obtained with different enzyme preps, they all have a** _**k**_ **cat of about 1 s[-1] for the control.**
**We have provided the amount of FAD bound in each of the Figure 2 panels in the figure legend of Figure 2.  We believe that the amount of FAD bound is relatively constant, and all**
**of these values are within the margin of error.  (The amount of ATP bound is much more difficult to measure.)**
It would also be helpful if the authors could measure the K_d values for FAD vs. ATP.

**In our original manuscript, we measured the activity of the apo enzyme in the presence of ATP and varying amounts of FAD (Fig. 3b).  This data showed that there were two EC50s for FAD, one at 385 nM FAD and one at 177**  **M FAD.  In our revised manuscript, to provide more evidence that the high affinity site of the enzyme for FAD is dependent on ATP, we repeated this experiment in the absence of ATP.  Addition of FAD still gave two plateaus, but the lower EC50 was increased from 385 nM FAD to 13.0**  **M FAD.  Thus, the effect of ATP appears to be to increase the affinity of the high affinity FAD binding site while the low affinity FAD binding site does not appear to be significantly affected (although the large error bars at high FAD concentration make it difficult to make a definitive assessment).  We supply this data as a new Figure 3c.**

**To directly address the reviewer’s request, we have also developed a fluorescence polarization assay to calculate the** _**K**_ **D of FAD, by measuring fluorescence anisotropy of FAD in the presence of different amounts of apo ACOX-1.1 with and without ATP.  We also calculated the** _**K**_ **D of ATP.  These data have been added to the manuscript as a new Figure 3f and a new Figure 3g.  The** _**K**_ **D value of the high affinity FAD binding site (450 ± 60 nM) is consistent with the high affinity EC50 for FAD in the presence of ATP obtained in Figure 3b. The** _**K**_ **D of the enzyme for FAD in the absence of ATP is too high to enable accurate measurement using this assay.  The** _**K**_ **D of apo ACOX-1.1 for ATP is 20.7**  **M, which is roughly consistent with the ATP EC50.**
2. The authors may report all kinetic parameters including the Hill coefficient.

**We reported the** _**k**_ **cat values of holo enzyme in Figure 2c,d and the corresponding** _**K**_ **half values Figure S8.  We report the** _**k**_ **cat values for apo enzyme in Figure 3a and the corresponding** _**K**_ **half values in a new Figure S12.  The Hill coefficient is discussed below.**

Was the Hill coefficient constrained to 2.0? Why in all fitting? If so, why? Do the two subunits exhibit cooperative behavior in the kinetics, or between substrate and FAD binding, or is this a misunderstanding of the reviewer? Further clarification on this point is needed.

**Our data indicate that there is cooperative binding of substrate between the two subunits. Furthermore, our data indicate that there is likely cooperative binding of FAD, as well as cooperative binding of ATP.  We have modified our model for binding of the enzyme to FAD and ATP, and we have clarified this model in the text.  Regarding the constraints placed on**

**the Hill coefficient, we have added the following explanatory text to the Methods: “For Fig. 2c, where seven different substrate concentrations were tested for each of the conditions, the average Hill coefficient was 1.75 ± 0.12.  Because it was not practical to test this number of substrate concentrations in all cases, the Hill coefficient was constrained to 2 for Fig. 2a-2d and Fig. 3a, as the data could not always be fitted without setting some constraints.  For Fig. 3b and Fig. 3c, where the FAD concentration was varied, the Hill coefficient for the first EC50 was 2.6 and 2.8, respectively.  Because it was difficult to measure the second EC50 at high FAD concentrations, the Hill coefficient was set to 2 for Fig. 3b and Fig. 3c to enable fitting of the data.  For Fig. 3d, where ATP concentration was varied, the Hill coefficient was 1.9. Thus, in both Fig. 3d and Fig. 3e, the Hill coefficient was set to 2 to enable fitting of the data in Fig. 3e, in which a high FAD concentration was used, resulting in large error bars.”**

3. Elaborate how the release of FAD is associated with the reaction. Given the proposed fast binding of FAD and ATP and considering their intracellular concentration, the implication of the allosteric regulation of ATP remains unclear. Are there any physiological situation where intracellular ATP concentration drops below 300 uM?

**We have added some additional data to this revision to confirm that the apo enzyme is dimeric even at the low enzyme concentrations at which we typically run our kinetic assays. Specifically, we have added dynamic light scattering (DLS) of wild-type apo ACOX-1.1, which shows that the apo enzyme is dimeric under the same conditions where we observe a synergistic enhancement of enzymatic activity by FAD and ATP (new Fig. S13).  We have further confirmed that the apo enzyme is dimeric using size exclusion chromatographymulti-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) analysis (new Fig. S14).  Thus, ATP can immediately enhance the activity of the dimeric enzyme.**

**At the same time, the rate of dissociation of the enzyme from FAD and ATP appears to be slow.  To better characterize this rate of dissociation, we monitored the fluorescence anisotropy of the FAD associated with wild-type holo ACOX-1.1 (new Fig. 2g).  This data suggests that the half-life for FAD dissociation from the enzyme is about 20 minutes. Interestingly, when we performed a similar assay for the holo ACOX-1.1 catalytic mutant (E434A), the half-life for FAD dissociation from the enzyme is much slower, about one hour.  This result is consistent with the fact that we typically purify this mutant with a higher level of bound FAD and ATP than we do wild-type enzyme.**

**Additional unknown factors in vivo may enhance the rate of dissociation of the enzyme from FAD and ATP.  For example, loss of FAD and ATP may be associated with substrate turnover, given that the catalytic mutant appears to bind more tightly to FAD and ATP. We have provided additional discussion of these possible factors in the discussion.**

**There are examples of physiological situations where intracellular ATP drops below 300**  **M.  We have elaborated upon this issue in the discussion and included new references.  We describe the information in the references in detail here:    In yeast and mammalian cells, ATP levels are in the mM range and are relatively constant (** _**J. Cell Sci**_ **., 2019, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1711497115; bioRxiv, 2021, 10.1101/2021.10.08.463131).   Meanwhile, in bacteria and in certain plant organelles and tissues, ATP levels vary a lot and can drop to the low**  **M range.   Yaginuma et al. showed that the concentration of ATP in individual bacteria can vary widely, with about 10% having less than 500**  **M (** _**Sci. Rep**_ **, 2024, DOI: 10.1038/srep06522).  Voon et al. showed that the ATP concentration of specific organelles (plastids) is quite low (200**  **M), due to high ATP consumption in the chloroplasts (** _**PNAS**_ **, 2018, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1711497115).  Gout at al. showed that the concentration of ATP in the cytosol of sycamore cells was about 450**  **M (** _**PNAS**_ **, 2014, 10.1073/pnas.1406251111).  To our knowledge, the absolute concentration of ATP in various organelles and tissues in** _**C. elegans**_ **has not been reported; there are only data on the concentration per mg protein or per worm and on the relative concentrations of ATP under different conditions.   For example, Hibshman et al. showed that ATP levels drop about 75% during starvation of the third larval (L3) stage for several days (** _**Am. J. Physiol. Cell Physiol.**_ **, 2018, DOI: 10.1152/ajpcell.00109.2018).**

**Importantly, other enzymes that are activated by ATP have** _**K**_ **D’s for ATP that are in the low- to mid-micromolar.  For example, a classic example, aspartate carbamoyltransferase, which is activated by ATP, has a high-affinity** _**K**_ **D for ATP of about 100-200**  **M (** _**JBC**_ **, 1973, DOI: 10.1016/S0021-9258(19)43510-2;** _**Biochemistry**_ **, 1975; DOI: 10.1021/bi00673a005). This information has been added to the discussion with references.**
4. In Figure 5, subunit A appears to have a larger tendency to open compared to subunit B, e.g., (i) apo, (iv) FAD_A/apoB vs. (v) apoA/FAD_B, and (vi) holoA/apoB. Any reason?

**This asymmetry is due to the stochastic nature of the opening event. To test this hypothesis, we have focused on the apo enzyme and increased our MD simulations to 20 replicates and also extended them, resulting in reducing asymmetry.  Additionally, by increasing the symmetry of the starting structure (replicating waters across subunits), we eliminated asymmetry of the simulations.  These new data appear in the revised Figure 5.  Our MD simulations have enabled us to identify a mechanism whereby the dimeric apo enzyme can bind to ATP, even though the ATP binding site is buried.**

In addition, was there any observed correlation between site opening and fluctuation of bound ligand? If not, what is the basis for believing that the site opening is relevant to ligand binding/release?

**Our primary evidence that site opening is related to fluctuation in bound FAD/ATP is that the apo enzyme shows opening of the ATP site and it responds (in terms of enzyme activity) to the addition of ATP plus FAD.**
## Minor:
1. For the MD simulation section, provides details on each system size, dimensions and the number of waters in each system.
**We have added a new Table S2, which provides details on each system size, dimensions, and the number of waters in each system.**
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):

This paper describes the study into the mechanism of allosteric regulation of C. elegans ACOX1.1 by ATP. Using combined experimental and MD simulations, the authors pinpointed the role of ATP on regulating the activity of ACOX enzyme by increasing its affinity to the FAD cofactor and proposed a potential entry-exit mechanism for ATP. The findings are interesting and the manuscript well written. There are several concerns with the MD simulations analysis which should be addressed before it is suitable for publication:

1. To illustrate the conformational changes associated with ATP and FAD binding, authors compared the representative frames from MD simulations of the apo state with the crystal structure of the holo form. I see that the authors have also conducted MD simulations for the holo dimer, therefore, any conformational changes associated with ATP binding should be compared between MD representative frames from MD simulations of both apo and holo forms. It is not appropriate to compare MD frames with the crystal structure of a different form, especially given that the apo crystal structure doesn’t show the same conformational change when compared with the holo crystal structure. It is possible that when apo structure is subjected to the freedom in MD simulations, they tend to open and relax, and the same could also happen to the holo state if it was subjected to the same degrees of freedom. The observed differences between MD frames and holo crystal structures may not reflect the true extent of conformational changes (or lack of).

**The purpose of Figure 4 was to illustrate the possible path for ATP and FAD entry/exit. The crystal structure does not have such a path for ATP entry/exit.  To illustrate the overall movement of the apo and holo enzymes in an unbiased matter, we have calculated the size of the ATP and FAD openings and graphed these distances throughout the MD simulations in Figure 5.**

2. Page 13, line 276-278, authors claimed that the only chance for ATP to bind to the dimer interface is to the apo dimer, however, looking at figures 5a (iv) and (v), which represents FAD_A/apoB and apoA/FAD_B systems, they appear to show some opening (~5 Å) of the ATP binding site as well. How big should the biding site opening be, to enable ATP entrance? Can authors show evidence that the ATP binding site must open beyond 5 Å for ATP entrance?

**Given the stochastic nature of the opening of the ATP sites, we decided to focus on the MD simulations of the apo and holo enzymes.  We increased the number of simulations as well as extended the length of the simulations, thereby reducing the asymmetry of the simulations.  Furthermore, by increasing the symmetry of the starting apo structure (by replicating the waters between the two subunits), we eliminated any asymmetry of the simulations. These new data appear in the revised Figure 5.**

**Due to the stochastic nature of the opening of the ATP sites, we feel that it is difficult to interpret the results of the hybrid systems (such as FAD_A/apoB and apoA/FAD_B) that were analyzed in our original manuscript.  Extending all of these systems to 20 simulations and beyond 2**  **s is beyond our computing resources.  Our main purpose with the MD simulations is to identify a mechanism whereby the dimeric apo enzyme can bind to ATP, even though the ATP binding site is buried.  Our MD simulations of the apo enzyme uncover this mechanism.**

3. Page 13, line 280-281, “once ATP and FAD both bind to subunit A, the dimer only shows opening for the FAD sites on the subunits A and B”, but judging by Figure 5b (vi), the FAD site is not open in subunit B?
**Please see our response to Remark #2.**

4. In general, it is not clear how MD have shown selective binding of ATP to one subunit (page 13 line 282), if ATP can only bind to the apo form, and the asymmetry in apo system was due to limited sampling in MD simulations.

**As described in Remark #2, for the MD simulations of the apo and holo enzymes, we increased the number of simulations, extended the simulation, and increased the symmetry of the starting structure in order to eliminate any overall asymmetry in the simulations. Thus, with sufficient sampling, we show that the ATP site on subunit A is as likely to open as the ATP site on subunit B.  Based on reevaluation of our original experimental data, and acquisition of new experimental data, we believe that both subunits of the enzyme can bind to ATP in a cooperative fashion.  Please find a full description of our revised model in our response to Reviewer #3’s Remark #10.**

5. One curious observation from Figure 5, is the opening of the FAD sites across different systems, even with FAD bound in the subunits. Can authors explain why this happens, shouldn’t bound FAD stabilize the binding site and maintain a closed conformation? On a related issue, later on in the manuscript, page 14 line 319-320, authors proposed that binding of FAD promote closure of the lid that caps the FAD site, however, the observed distances in Figure 5 do not support this.

**We thank the reviewer for pointing this inconsistency out. By increasing the number of simulations and focusing on the apo to holo comparison, we do observe less opening of both the ATP and FAD sites in the holo enzyme in comparison to the apo enzyme.  Please see the revised Figure 5.**

6. Authors identified several residues that are supposedly in the allosteric network and important for the allosteric regulation of ACOX by ATP, has any of these network residues been tested by mutagenesis for their contribution to the ATP allosteric mechanism?

**We have mutated several residues in the allosteric network and assayed the activity of the mutant enzymes.  Specifically, the R343A, R343Q, N437A, K391N, R295A, and R295Q mutants have been made and characterized. Although the mutants are well folded by CD spectroscopy, they all have very low activity, they bind very little FAD, and their activity is not affected by ATP.  We have included these data in new figures, including Fig. 6e-6h and Fig. S13-S15.  Thus, we have provided experimental evidence for the allosteric network.**
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Comments:

In this study, the authors employed biochemical and molecular dynamic simulation techniques to investigate the effect of ATP on the enzymatic activity of C. elegans acyl-CoA oxidase 1.1 (ACOX-1.1). They found that ATP moderately enhances the binding affinity of ACOX-1.1 for the cofactor FAD, thereby stimulating enzymatic activity. This effect is highly specific, as other nucleotides do not induce a similar effect. Molecular dynamics simulation of the apo ACOX-1.1 structure revealed a hydrogen-bonding network linking the ATP and FAD binding sites. Based on these results, the authors proposed a molecular mechanism for the effect of ATP: the binding of ATP to the enzyme allosterically enhances the binding of FAD, thereby enhancing the enzymatic activity.

Significance: The findings of this study are incremental and may not hold sufficient significance for a broader audience. While they may be of interests to researchers working in the biochemical studies of ACOX, the biological implications of the results have not been adequately explored.

**We used CRISPR-Cas9 to generate a worm strain expressing a mutant ACOX.1-1 (H396G), which showed defects in pheromone production in the worm. Our current data provide a mechanism whereby this mutation would affect FAD binding and thus activity of the enzyme.  We are the first to show regulation of an oxidase by ATP in vitro and in vivo. We have provided further description of phenotype of the ACOX-1.1(H396G) mutant worm strain in the manuscript.**

Methodology: Overall, the methodology is generally sound, and the authors have provided sufficient details. However, some experiments and analyses are not well performed. Additionally, the major conclusions are not well supported by data.

**Unfortunately, we believe based on our reading of the reviewer’s critique that their copy of our manuscript was missing Figure 3, which contained critical data on the effect of FAD and ATP on the activity of the apo enzyme.  We elaborate on the data found in Figure 3, as well as additional data that we have added to the revised manuscript, in our responses to the reviewer below.**
Critique:

1. In the enzymatic assay, the authors used a purified enzyme with about 50% of the enzyme bound with FAD. It would be more appropriate to use the apo enzyme, which has no bound FAD and exhibits no activity. With this apo enzyme, the authors should add a fixed amount of FAD in the reaction to measure all kinetic parameters, as the authors indicated that the amount of bound FAD varies between batches of purified enzyme, which would affect the enzymatic activity. Additionally, the authors should use this “real” apo enzyme as a reference for analyzing the effects of FAD, ATP, and FAD+ATP.
## **We believe that the reviewer was not aware of our analysis of the apo enzyme, which appeared in Figure 3 in the original manuscript.**

Furthermore, in the enzymatic activity assay, the authors primarily measured the kcat of the catalytic reaction. They should also measure Vmax, Km for both the substrate and FAD (which represent the apparent binding affinities for the substrate and FAD, respectively), and the Hill coefficient for the substrate (which indicates the number of substrate binding sites in the dimeric enzyme).

**We provided the** _**K**_ **m values associated with Figure 2c,d in Figure S8, and we provide the** _**K**_ **m values associated with Figure 3a as a new Fig. S12.  Vmax is equivalent to a** _**k**_ **cat that has not been normalized for the amount of enzyme used in the reaction, and thus** _**k**_ **cat is a more**

**useful number than Vmax.  In the original submission, we provided in Figure 3b the EC50 of the enzyme for FAD the presence of ATP.  This data showed that there is a high affinity site for FAD (presumably due to bound ATP) and a low affinity site for FAD.  In the revised manuscript, we have also provided a new Figure 3c, in which we provide the EC50 of the enzyme for FAD in the absence of ATP.  This data shows that the EC50 of the high affinity site for FAD shifts dramatically from about 385 nM to 13.0**  **M, while the low affinity site for FAD does not shift.  This result suggests that ATP binding is responsible for the creation of the high affinity FAD binding site.  In response to Reviewer #1, we have also developed a fluorescent polarization assay to measure the** _**K**_ **D of the enzyme for FAD and ATP and added this data to the revised manuscript as a new Figure 3f,g.  These data confirm that there is a high affinity site for FAD only in the presence of ATP.  We have provided the Hill coefficient for substrate (Hill coefficient = 1.75) in the manuscript text.**

2. Page 4, 2nd paragraph: The orientation of Fig. 1b is awkward, making it difficult for readers to see the  K helix. Additionally, the authors did not include the catalytic residue E434 in the catalytic loop. From Fig. 1b, we can see that H396 is involved in the ATP binding; however, K391 and N437 are not involved in the binding. What are the functional roles of these two residues in the ATP binding or FAD binding?

**Unfortunately, we think the depicted image in Figure 1b is the only orientation that enables a clear view of all of the residues that we reference in the text.  We believe that this view makes it clear that the**  **L helix is in the foreground, the**  **K helix is in the background, and the catalytic loop connects the two.  We did not depict the catalytic residue because this figure is an overlay of apo wild-type ACOX-1.1 (white) and the holo ACOX-1.1(E434A) mutant (orange/cyan).  In the apo structure the catalytic loop does not have defined electron density (and thus appears as a hashed white tube), and in the holo structure the catalytic Glu has been mutated to Ala.  We have added the following text to the Figure 1b legend:  “The catalytic residue, E434, is not depicted in the catalytic loop in this figure because it is mutated to Ala in the holo ACOX-1.1(E434A) structure, and it is disordered in the apo ACOX-1.1 structure.”  The roles of K391 and N437 are described in the manuscript text, and we provide the relevant text to the reviewer: “In the ACOX-1.1(E434A) structure, we identified a hydrogen bond network between the FAD and ATP binding sites involving two critical residues, K391 and N437, that likely stabilize the catalytic loop that connects two**  **-helices (**  **K and**  **L) and contains the catalytic residue, E434 (Fig. 1b).  On the other hand, in the wild-type ACOX-1.1 apo-structure, which is not bound to either FAD or ATP, there is no electron density for K391, N437, or the catalytic loop.  Single residue mutations to K391, N437, or distal residues in either the ATP or FAD binding sites resulted in a lack of retention of both ATP and FAD during purification, suggesting that ATP and FAD binding are correlated.”**

3. Page 5, lines 110-114: The authors state that “Specifically, for wild-type enzyme, using a similar purification method as is described here, roughly 50% of the enzyme is bound to FAD and slightly less is bound to ATP, for the E434A catalytic mutant, roughly 100% of enzyme is bound to FAD and ATP, and for a variety of mutants in either the FAD or ATP binding sites, none of the enzyme is bound to either FAD or ATP.” What are the mutants which lost the ability to bind either FAD or ATP?

**We have added a reference to the sentence that the reviewer is highlighting to our paper on the structure of ACOX-1.1 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1608262113).  In this reference, we showed that the ACOX-1.1(N437A) and ACOX-1.1(K391A) mutants bind little to no ATP and FAD, consistent with the role of Asn437 and Lys391 in coordinating the binding of ATP and FAD.  ACOX-1.1(W536A), which is lacking a Trp residue that stacks with the isoalloxazine ring of FAD, fails to bind FAD or ATP.   ACOX-1.1(Q340A), which is lacking a Gln located on αH that hydrogen bonds to the ribose ring of FAD, also fails to bind both FAD and ATP.**

In a later biochemical study (page 10), the authors only examined the binding abilities (FAD and ATP binding abilities) of the H396G and R536E mutants. Do these mutants exhibit any enzymatic activity in the absence and presence of FAD, ATP, and FAD+ATP?

**We believe that the reviewer was not aware of this data, which was shown in Figure 3e,f of the original submission.  This data now appears in Figure 3h,i of the revised submission. The ACOX-1.1(H396G) and ACOX-1.1(R536E) mutants purify without any bound FAD and are completely inactive unless FAD is included in the enzymatic reaction buffer, in which case they have only a low level of activity.  Not surprisingly, both the ACOX1.1(H396G) mutant and the ACOX-1.1(R536E) mutant do not respond to ATP.  Thus, the effects of ATP on ACOX-1.1 affinity for FAD are specifically due to it binding to the ATP binding sites on ACOX-1.1.**
Since R536 is involved in binding of the α and β phosphates of ATP, it should also be included in Fig. 1b. (The authors cited Fig. 1b in discussing R536E on page 10, 2nd paragraph.)
## **We have added R536 to Figure 1b.**

4. Page 6, lines 116-117: The authors state that “the enzyme with added FAD and ATP had only a slightly enhanced amount of FAD bound and enzymatic activity than enzyme that was purified using our standard method (Fig. S1b).” Fig. S1b only shows the kcat of the enzyme under different purification conditions, and does not provide information on the amount of FAD bound.

**It is difficult to accurately measure the amount of FAD bound to the enzyme that was purified with FAD in the size exclusion chromatography buffer.  The problem is that FAD is in the buffer, and we cannot purify the enzyme from the FAD in the buffer without possibly altering the amount of FAD bound to the enzyme.  Therefore, we altered the text to read: “However, the enzyme with added FAD and ATP had only slightly enhanced enzymatic activity in comparison to enzyme that was purified using our standard method.”**

5. On page 6, lines 124-126: The authors state that “Addition of 10 μM FAD and 350 μM ATP to the enzymatic reaction did not lead to an immediate enhancement of the activity of ACOX-1.1 (Fig. S1b).” On page 7, lines 149-150: The authors also state that “the FAD and ATP can immediately rescue the time-dependent decrease in activity that is otherwise seen (Fig. 2b).” These two statements appear to contradict each other.

**If we incubate the purified enzyme (which is purified with about 50% of the protein bound to FAD/ATP) at room temperature, it gradually becomes apo.  It is this apo enzyme that responds immediately to FAD and ATP.  According to our model, once the enzyme has become apo, a high affinity FAD binding site is available to respond immediately to low concentrations of FAD in the presence of ATP.  For further description of our model and how our data support this model, please see our response to your Remark # 10.**

6. Page 7, lines 157-158: The authors state that “None of these nucleotides are able to rescue the time-dependent decrease in enzymatic activity (Fig. 2d).” Fig. 2d does not exhibit a timedependent change.

**These samples were incubated for one hour at room temperature in the presence of either nothing, FAD, FAD plus ATP, or FAD plus other nucleotides, and the enzyme’s activity was assayed.  This incubation normally leads to a decrease in activity as shown in Figure 2a. However, FAD plus ATP was able to rescue this decrease better than FAD plus any other tested nucleotide.  To clarify the manuscript, we have added some additional text to the figure legend.**
Additionally, in the presence of FAD+deoxy-ATP or FAD+GTP, the kcat value is moderately increased compared to that in the presence of only FAD. Therefore, this statement is imprecise.
**We make the statement more precise by adding the underlined text: “None of these nucleotides are able to rescue the time-dependent decrease in enzymatic activity as well as ATP.”**
7. Page 8, line 1: 100 μM FAD is needed to reach a similar effect as 10 μM FAD+500 μM ATP.
What are the concentrations of FAD and ATP under the cellular conditions at which the catalytic reaction takes place?
**As described in our response to Reviewer #1, we have added additional information and references to the manuscript’s discussion on the concentrations of ATP and FAD in the cell.**
**The following text appears in the discussion:**

**“The EC50’s of ACOX-1.1 for FAD and ATP are potentially consistent with a model in which cellular concentrations of FAD and ATP regulate the activity of the enzyme** _**in vivo**_ **. In yeast and mammalian cells, ATP concentration is reported to be relatively stable and to be in the low mM range.[28,29] In contrast, in bacteria, ATP concentration has been found to significantly fluctuate and to be less than 500**  **M in about 10% of cells.[30] Furthermore, in certain organelles and tissues of plants, ATP concentration is reported in the low- to midmicromolar range.[31,32] In** _**C. elegans**_ **, ATP concentration has only been reported as a relative number; for example, Hibshman** _**et al.**_ **showed that ATP levels drop about 75% during starvation for several days.[33] Thus, it is unknown what the concentration of ATP is in different organelles and tissues in** _**C. elegans**_ **.  The** _**K**_ **D of ATP-regulated allosteric sites in enzymes ranges from the low micromolar to low millimolar range.[34-36] For example, the** _**K**_ **D of the high affinity ATP site of the ATP-activated aspartate transcarbamoylase for ATP is in the 100-200**  **M range.[37] The concentration of free (non-protein-bound) FAD has also been demonstrated to fluctuate, but is typically reported to be in the low micromolar range.[38-40] Our data would suggest that if the ATP concentration is below the EC50 that we detected for ACOX-1.1 (88.8 ± 8.6**  **M), FAD concentrations would have to be in the hundred micromolar range in order to activate the enzyme, which is a much higher concentration than is typically reported for the cell.  Thus, sufficient ATP in** _**C. elegans**_ **would potentially enable ACOX-1.1 to utilize its high affinity, nanomolar FAD binding site.  However, it is not known whether ATP concentrations dip low enough in** _**C. elegans**_ **for ATP to enable this type of regulatory mechanism.”**

8. Page 8, last paragraph: The authors suggest that substrate turnover enhances FAD/ATP release. This appears to contradict the established catalytic mechanism. The catalytic mechanism of ACOX has been thoroughly studied and well understood. Following the catalytic reaction, reduced FAD is oxidized by molecular oxygen to form oxidized FAD, which then reenters the next cycle of the catalytic reaction rather than dissociating from the enzyme. Additionally, the enzymatic activity upon the addition of substrate second time in the presence of both ATP and FAD appears weaker than that upon the addition of substrate first time (Fig. 2g). This suggests that the decreased activity of the enzyme may be due to some unknown factors, such as incomplete release of the product, enzyme denaturation, interference of the UV signal for FAD in the assay (page 10, line 212), or other possibilities.

**We agree with the reviewer that there are limitations to this assay, since it could be complicated by factors such as product inhibition.  We have removed from the current manuscript the original Fig. 2g.  We do believe that the off rate of the enzyme for FAD/ATP could be influenced by catalysis, since the catalytic mutant (E434A) is normally purified with a high percentage of bound FAD/ATP.  Additionally, we have added a new figure to the current manuscript showing that the E434A mutant is slow to release bound FAD/ATP. Additional factors may stimulate the off rate of ACOX-1.1 for FAD/ATP in vivo, and we have added additional discussion of possible factors to the manuscript’s discussion.**
9. Page 9, 2nd paragraph: The authors cited Fig. 3. In the merged manuscript, there is only the caption of Fig. 3, but no figure. Instead, Fig. 5 is shown twice.

**In our copy of the merged original manuscript, Figure 3 is shown, and Figure 5 is not shown twice.  Unfortunately, there appears to have been a problem with the version of the merged manuscript that Reviewer #3 received.**

10. Page 9, last paragraph: Based on the biochemical data (EC50), the authors propose that the dimeric enzyme of ACOX-1.1 possesses both a high affinity binding site and a low affinity binding site for FAD. ATP binds to one subunit of the dimeric enzyme, creating a high-affinity FAD binding site on that subunit, but does not bind to the other subunit, resulting in a lowaffinity FAD binding site on the other subunit. This proposal appears to contradict to the structural data. So far, there is no structure of ACOX showing that the dimeric enzyme has an asymmetric composition with two subunits in different conformations and bound to different ligands (such as FAD and ATP).

**When we purify the wild-type ACOX-1.1, it has roughly 50% FAD and ATP bound, and we cannot stimulate the activity of the enzyme through the addition of 10**  **M FAD and 350**  **M ATP.  Furthermore, when we generate apo ACOX-1.1, we observe two EC50s for FAD, indicating a high affinity FAD binding site and a low affinity binding site.  The high affinity FAD binding site is likely created by the binding of ATP to the enzyme.**

**In our original and revised manuscript, we proposed two possible models: (1) a certain fraction of the enzyme is purified with cofactors and is active while a certain fraction is purified without cofactors and is inactive, or (2) only one subunit in the dimer is bound to cofactors and is active while the other is not. Based on the reviewers’ suggestions, reevaluation of our original data, and acquisition of new data, we believe that the first model is more likely the correct one.**
**The reason that the first model is more likely is due to the following: (1) We observe a Hill coefficient of 1.75 for substrate, indicating that the two subunits of the enzyme bind**
**cooperatively to substrate.  (2) We observe cooperative binding of FAD by the two subunits of the enzyme.  (3) We observe cooperative binding of ATP by the two subunits of the enzyme.**

**Thus, for Figure 3b, we believe that there are two populations of enzyme, one that is responsible for the high affinity EC50 for which the two subunits of the enzyme cooperatively bind to FAD in the presence of ATP, and another that is responsible for the low affinity EC50 for which the two subunits weakly bind to FAD and likely do not bind to ATP.**
**We have clarified which model our data support in the text of the revised manuscript.**
In addition, besides the EC50 measurements, could the authors employ another method to confirm that the dimeric enzyme has both a high affinity binding site and a low affinity binding site for FAD?

**As mentioned in a response to an earlier critique, we have developed a fluorescence polarization assay to measure the** _**K**_ **D of the enzyme for FAD and ATP and added this data to the revised manuscript as a new Figure 3f,g.  These data confirm that there is a high affinity site for FAD only in the presence of ATP.  The assay cannot confirm the low affinity site since the enzyme (not FAD) is in excess in this assay.**

11. In the MD simulations, the authors started from the apo structure, and the results showed that the FAD binding sites opened to some extent, while the ATP binding sites opened in a much more stochastic manner (Fig. S10). This seems somewhat unusual, as the apo structure has open conformations for both the FAD and ATP binding sites, the simulations should demonstrate that these open conformations would tend to transition to closed conformations to some degree.

**When we extend the number and length of the MD simulations for the apo structure, we show that these open conformations can transition to a closed conformation.  We have added a new Fig. S17, showing a closeup of the ATP sites in selected MD simulations.  In almost all simulations, the enzyme transitions back and forth rapidly between an ATP open and closed conformation.**

Furthermore, the authors should consider conducting MD simulations starting with the holo structure with the bound FAD and ATP removed, to observe how the FAD and ATP binding sites undergo conformational changes.
**The problem with this type of simulation is that when we remove the FAD and ATP, we have to somewhat arbitrarily place waters in the FAD and ATP binding sites.**
12. In the MD simulations, the authors also conducted simulations for several artificially

constructed models, such as ATP-A/apoB, apoA/ATP-B, FAD-A/apoB, apoA/FAD-B, holoA/ApoB, and apoA/holoB (Fig. 5). Theoretically, each pair of models (such as ATP-A/apoB and apoA/ATP-B) is essentially similar or identical (depending on how the structures of the dimeric enzymes were solved: i.e. whether the asymmetric unit contains a dimer or a monomer which forms a dimer with a symmetry related monomer). Consequently, the simulation results for each pair should be comparable.

**Given the stochastic nature of the opening of the ATP sites, we decided to focus on the MD simulations of the apo and holo enzymes.  We increased the number of simulations as well as extended the length of the simulations, thereby reducing the asymmetry of the simulations.  Furthermore, by increasing the symmetry of the starting structure (by replicating the waters between the two subunits), we eliminated any asymmetry of the simulations. These new data appear in the revised Figure 5.  Our MD simulations have enabled us to identify a mechanism whereby the dimeric apo enzyme can bind to ATP, even though the ATP binding site is buried.**

13. Based on the MD simulation of the apo ACOX-1.1 structure, the authors identified a hydrogen-bonding network connecting the ATP and FAD binding sites and proposed a molecular mechanism for the effect of ATP: the binding of ATP to the enzyme can allosterically enhance the binding of FAD, thereby potentiating the enzymatic activity. However, this finding lacks structural data to support. Previously, the structures of ACOX-1.1 in apo form and the E434A ACOX-1.1 mutant in complex with both FAD and ATP have been solved.

**The allosteric network was identified by comparing the MD simulations of the holo and apo enzymes using a program SenseNet.  We are not certain what the reviewer means by our allosteric network lacking structural support.  In the crystal structure of the catalytic (E434A) mutant, a series of residues connect the ATP binding site and the FAD binding site. In the crystal structure of the wild-type apo enzyme, the catalytic loop is disordered.  Many of the relevant residues in the allosteric network are present in this loop.  The disorder in the loop argues that this loop is part of the allosteric network as it needs FAD and ATP to be ordered.**

**In our revised manuscript, we have provided additional support for this allosteric network by mutating several key residues in the allosteric network and assaying the enzymatic activity of the mutant enzymes.  As described in our respond to Reviewer#2, the R343A, R343Q, N437A, K391N, R295A, and R295Q mutants have been made and characterized. Although the mutants are well folded by CD spectroscopy, they all have very low activity, they bind very little FAD, and their activity is not affected by ATP.  We have added these data in new figures, including Fig. 6e-6h and Fig. S19-S21.**

Additionally, the structures of human ACOX1a in apo form and in complex with FAD have also been solved. These structures would enable the authors to analyze the conformational changes of the enzymes, particularly at the active sites, the FAD binding sites, and the ATP binding sites, caused by the binding of FAD and the binding of ATP. Such an analysis should clarify whether the binding of ATP enhances the binding of FAD compared to the FAD-bound structure and provide the molecular basis for the biochemical results indicating that the ATP binding increases the binding affinity of the enzyme for FAD.

**We do not believe that ATP binds human ACOX1a.  Comparison of the binding sites of** _**C. elegans**_ **ACOX-1.1 to hACOX1a indicates that the hACOX1a is missing residues that would be needed for binding ATP.  Furthermore, in unpublished work, we have been unable to detect any dependence of hACOX1a activity on ATP.  Interestingly, however, there is an enclosed cavity in hACOX1a in the same location as the ATP binding site of** _**C. elegans**_ **ACOX-1.1, but it is unclear whether this cavity binds to anything or has a function.**
14. Many of the structure figures are overly crowded (such as Fig. 1a, Fig. 3c, and Fig. 6a), and lack some of the information discussed in the text.

**We made the cartoon depiction in Figure 1a more transparent, and we provided a larger version of Figure 6a in the SI as a new Figure S18.  Figure 3c is a graph, so we are not sure what the reviewer is referring to.**
The authors addressed the comments by the reviewer and the reviewer has no additional comments.

The revised manuscript has addressed most of my previous comments, and I appreciate the authors' efforts to increase the sampling in the MD simulations. However, a key issue remains with Figure 4, where the authors attempt to identify an entry/exit mechanism for FAD and ATP. The comparison between the MD representative structure of the apo enzyme and the holo crystal structure is problematic, as these two structures are not directly comparable.

Crystal structures of both the apo and holo forms do not capture the conformational changes that give rise to the entry/exit mechanism. This suggests that both crystal forms are constrained by crystal packing effects. In contrast, the MD simulations allow the apo form to open up, as well as the FAD site in the holo form (as shown in Figure 5). Therefore, the closed conformation of the holo crystal structure does not accurately represent the binding sites when both FAD and ATP are present.

The authors mention in the manuscript that comparing crystal structures does not reveal the entry/exit mechanism, and as such, a more appropriate comparison would be between the MD representative conformations of both the holo and apo forms. Given the wide spread distances sampled in the MD simulations of the holo form, especially the FAD binding site, authors may be able to identify several representative conformations depending on the method of clustering and criteria for selecting these frames.

Additionally, the authors should provide further detail on how the MD representative conformations were selected, including the criteria used to ensure the structural relevance and accuracy of these conformations.

**We appreciate the reviewer’s comments, and in response, we have performed clustering analysis of the MD simulations to select representative frames corresponding to open and closed states.  As described in a new “Clustering Analysis” section of the Methods, we obtained eight subsets in total for the apo and holo systems in either the closed or open states of the ATP and FAD sites. Each subset was clustered using a hierarchical agglomerative algorithm based on the similarity of the relevant ligand binding sites.  In each subset of frames, the centroid of the cluster with the highest population was selected as the representative structure.  We have revised Figure 4 such that we are comparing the representative structures of the closed and open states of the FAD and ATP**

**sites of the apo enzyme.  This data confirms our proposed mechanism for FAD and ATP entry/exit from the apo enzyme.  For a comparative analysis of the ligand binding site flexibility between the apo and holo systems, we calculated the ligand binding site opening distances of the centroids for the top 10 clusters, and this data is shown as a new Figure S18.  We have also overlaid the representative FAD open structures for the apo and holo enzymes and the representative ATP open structures for the apo and holo enzymes, and this data is shown as a new Figure S19.  This data confirms that the FAD and ATP sites are more closed in the holo enzyme than in the apo enzyme.**
The authors have more or less incorporated my comments in the revision. I support publication now.

## ATP allosterically regulates an acyl-CoA oxidase

Butcher 1 Accepted: 7 July 2025 ATP is an important allosteric regulator of many enzymes, but these enzymes Check for updates typically utilize ATP or other nucleotides as substrates. Acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX) enzymes are central players in peroxisomal fatty acid metabolism, as well as in secondary metabolism in nematodes and plants. These dimeric enzymes have been shown to bind to ATP at unusual sites that are buried at the dimer interface. Here, we show that ATP stimulates the activity of an ACOX enzyme by increasing the binding affinity of the enzyme for its FAD cofactor. The effect of ATP is highly specific as other nucleotides do not stimulate the activity of the enzyme and mutation of the ATP binding site blocks the effect. We use X-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations of the apo dimeric enzyme to identify an unprecedented mechanism whereby ATP can reach its binding site through a shift in an α-helix bundle. Acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX) enzymes play a central role in primary metabolism, catalyzing the first and rate-limiting step in the peroxisomal β-oxidation cycle that shortens long-chain fatty acids, branched-chain fatty acids, and bile acid intermediates.

In humans, there are three ACOX enzymes (ACOX1, 2, and 3) with each specializing in different types of substrates[1][–][4] . The crystal structures of human ACOX1 and homologs from a variety of organisms reveal that these enzymes have a homodimeric structure with FAD cofactors noncovalently bound to each subunit at the dimeric interface. These enzymes use a two-step mechanism to install α,β-unsaturation in their acyl-CoA substrates. First, a catalytic glutamate abstracts the α-proton of the CoA-thioester, leading to hydride transfer from the β-position to FAD. Then, FADH2 is reoxidized through the reduction of molecular oxygen to form hydrogen peroxide[5][,][6] . In contrast, the mitochondrial counterpart to the peroxisomal ACOX enzymes, the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, transfer the electrons to FAD and ultimately the electron transport chain[7][,][8] . 

In addition to primary metabolism, ACOX enzymes participate in secondary metabolism in many organisms, including nematodes and plants[9][–][11] . In C. elegans, ACOX enzymes control the production of the ascaroside pheromones, a broad family of pheromones that mediate chemical communication in the worm, enabling it to coordinate its development and behavior[12] . There are seven C. elegans ACOX enzymes, with five of these directly implicated in ascaroside biosynthesis (ACOX-1.1, −1.2, −1.3, −1.4, and −3, referred to as ACOX-1, −2, −3, −4, and −6 in earlier literature)[13][–][17] . These enzymes act as gatekeepers in the β-oxidation cycle that shortens the side chains of the ascarosides. Different ACOX enzymes have different side-chain length preferences, leading to a diverse pool of ascarosides with different side-chain lengths. 

Remarkably, structural analysis of the ACOX enzymes from C.

elegans revealed that these enzymes have an ATP-binding site that is critical for enzymatic activity[15] . The crystal structures of ACOX-1.1 and ACOX-1.2 containing mutations in the catalytic glutamate (E434A and E432A, respectively) revealed that, in addition to FAD, these enzymes

## ATP modulates the affinity of ACOX-1.1 for FAD 

Incubation of ACOX-1.1 in the absence of added FAD or ATP results in a time-dependent decrease in enzymatic activity (Fig. 2a, b). Interestingly, this decrease can be prevented completely by including FAD and ATP in the incubation buffer, but can be prevented only partially by FAD alone (Fig. 2a). Importantly, the effects of FAD and ATP on enzyme activity are immediate. That is, if the enzyme is incubated for a period of time without FAD and ATP, such that its activity declines, and then FAD and ATP are added and enzyme activity immediately assayed, the FAD and ATP can immediately rescue the time-dependent decrease in activity that is otherwise seen (Fig. 2b). Thus, the time-dependent loss of activity is not due to degradation or unfolding of the enzyme. We confirmed the stability of the enzyme during the incubation by analyzing it by SDS-PAGE and circular dichroism before and after incubation (Supplementary Fig. 6). 

The kcat almost doubles utilizing enzyme that was incubated with FAD and ATP relative to enzyme that was not incubated with FAD and ATP (Fig. 2c).

The Hill coefficient averaged across conditions is equal to 1.75 ± 0.12, suggesting that the two subunits of the enzyme cooperatively bind substrate (Fig. 2c). To test the specificity of the effect of ATP on the rate of the enzyme, the incubation was repeated with FAD plus other nucleotides, including deoxy-ATP, ADP, AMP, and GTP. None of these nucleotides are able to rescue the time-dependent decrease in enzymatic activity as well as ATP (Fig. 2d). When utilizing 10 μM FAD, the concentration of ATP needed for half-maximal rescue is 248.7 μM (95% CI: 151.6–484.4 μM), and it plateaus at mid to high-μM ATP (Fig. 2e, f and Supplementary Fig. 7). To obtain a similar amount of rescue with FAD alone (that is, with no ATP), at least 100 μM FAD is needed, suggesting that ATP increases the affinity of the enzyme for FAD (Fig. 2e). Although the Khalf is not a direct measurement of substrate affinity, its minimal change in the presence of FAD and ATP suggests that FAD and ATP help to maintain the kcat during incubation 

but do not significantly affect the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate (Supplementary Fig. 8). 

The enzyme-coupled kinetic assay is an indirect measure of enzymatic activity. To confirm that the effect of ATP and FAD on rate is correlated to substrate turnover, a more direct assay for product formation based on HPLC was developed. These data confirmed that indeed ATP increases the rate of product formation (Supplementary Fig. 9a). It was also confirmed by HPLC that ATP is not hydrolyzed by ACOX-1.1, since the rate of ATP hydrolysis when ACOX-1.1 was incubated with ATP did not surpass that when ATP was incubated with FAD in the absence of enzyme (Supplementary Fig. 9b).

Thus, ATP can increase the rate of substrate turnover in the presence of FAD cofactor without the hydrolysis of ATP. 

To verify that the loss of enzyme activity during incubation was due to loss of FAD, we developed an assay to measure the koff based on the fluorescence anisotropy of FAD. Incubation of wild-type holo ACOX-1.1 led to a gradual decrease in anisotropy with a koff of 1.93 h[−][1] , indicating that roughly half of the bound FAD is lost in 20 minutes (Fig. 2g). ## Discussion 

Through X-ray crystallography, enzymology, and MD simulations, we have uncovered a unique role for ATP in the allosteric regulation of an oxidase enzyme. Previously, the structure of the ACOX-1.1(E434A) catalytic mutant homodimer suggested that the enzyme is bound to both its cofactor FAD and ATP at two symmetric sites at the interface between the two subunits, with one FAD/ATP primarily associated with each subunit[15] .

The ATP-binding sites in ACOX-1.1 do not resemble any previously identified conserved ATP-binding domain based on a search of two different databases, one of nucleotide binding domains and another of allosteric modulators[23][,][24] . Typically, ATP is bound by loop motifs that recognize the phosphates and/or adenine ring of ATP, but the ATPbinding domain in ACOX-1.1 has a purely helical fold made up of α-helices contributed by both subunits of the dimer[25][–][27] . Because these sites are buried at the dimer interface, our initial analysis of the crystal structure did not reveal how ATP might enter/exit its binding site, enabling it to allosterically regulate the enzyme. However, our MD simulations of wildtype apo ACOX-1.1 have revealed a potential mechanism whereby ATP could enter/exit the enzyme through the movement of an α-helix bundle. Furthermore, they have revealed a potential mechanism whereby FAD could enter/exit the enzyme through the movement of a β-sheet and associated loops, as well as an allosteric network through which ATP could allosterically regulate the binding of FAD.

Based on these simulations, the apo enzyme has sufficient flexibility to open the ATPbinding site through the movement of an α-helix bundle including αM, αL, and αN and to open the FAD-binding site through the movement of the β-sheet in which β1 and β2 reside. In contrast to the apo enzyme, which is potentially flexible enough to allow ATP binding, the holo-enzyme is almost completely closed at the ATP-binding sites. This result agrees with the slow off-rate of the holo enzyme for ATP and FAD. 

The EC50’s of ACOX-1.1 for FAD and ATP are potentially consistent with a model in which cellular concentrations of FAD and ATP regulate the activity of the enzyme in vivo. In yeast and mammalian cells, ATP concentration is reported to be relatively stable and to be in the lowmillimolar range[28][,][29] . In contrast, in bacteria, ATP concentration has been found to significantly fluctuate and to be less than 500 μM in about 10% of cells[30] .

Furthermore, in certain organelles and tissues of plants, ATP concentration is reported in the low-to-mid-micromolar range[31][,][32] . In C. elegans, to our knowledge, ATP concentration has only been reported as a relative number; for example, Hibshman et al. showed that ATP levels drop about 75% during starvation for several days[33] . Thus, it is unknownwhatthe concentration of ATPisindifferent organelles and tissues in C. elegans. The KD of ATP-regulated allosteric sites in enzymes ranges from the low-micromolar to low-millimolar range[34][–][36] . For example, the KD of the high-affinity ATP site of the ATPactivated aspartate transcarbamoylase is in the 100–200 μM range[37][,][38] . The concentration of free (non-protein-bound) FAD has also been demonstrated to fluctuate, but is typically reported to be in the lowmicromolar range[39][–][41] . Our data would suggest that if the ATP concentration is below the EC50 that we detected for ACOX-1.1 (about 69.4 μM), FAD concentrations would have to be in the hundred micromolar range in order to activate the enzyme, which is a much higher concentration than is typically reported for the cell. Thus, sufficient ATP in C. elegans would potentially enable ACOX-1.1 to utilize its high-affinity, nanomolar FAD-binding site. ## Enzyme-coupled kinetic assay 

The assay was adapted from a previously published protocol with modifications made to accommodate a 96-well plate setup[2] . In brief, the assay couples substrate-dependent hydrogen peroxide production by the enzyme to the formation of a UV-active product.

A standard curve of the concentration of hydrogen peroxide versus the measured signal at 500 nm yielded a molar absorption coefficient of 6900 M[−][1] cm[−][1] that is consistent with previous literature[1] . The assay buffer was the same as the size-exclusion running buffer, and the substrate used was lauroyl-CoA (C12-CoA). The substrate concentration was either held constant at 25 µM for initial rate measurements or varied from 3 or 5 µM to 50 µM for the determination of kinetic parameters. A minimum of seven substrate concentrations were used for experiments with a 1-h incubation, and a minimum of four substrate concentrations were used for other experiments. ACOX-1.1 was mixed with all components except substrate in a tube and then aliquoted to each well of a 96-well plate, and aliquoting after mixing the enzyme with the components was staggered in such a way that every replicate for each condition tested was incubated for an equivalent time. ## MD simulations 

To generate starting structures for MD simulations, the wild-type apo ACOX-1.1 and holo ACOX-1.1(E434A) crystal structures with Protein Data Bank (PDB) codes 5K3H and 5K3I, respectively, were downloaded from the RCSB PDB database[47] .

These structures contain four homodimers within the unit cell, but only one homodimer consisting of subunits A and B was used in this study. For the holo ACOX1.1(E434A), the structure includes FAD and ATP molecules bound to both subunits A and B. For the wild-type holo starting structure, the A434 residue in the holo ACOX-1.1(E434A) crystal structure was mutated in silico back to glutamate to make the structure wild-type in sequence. Because some residues are missing in both the apo and holo-crystal structures, these residues were built into the starting structures using AlphaFold2 and SWISS-MODEL, respectively[48][,][49] . For example, for the wild-type apo ACOX-1.1 starting structure, the catalytic loop including residues 431 to 436 was missing and thus was built into the apo starting structure using AlphaFold2 with apo ACOX-1.1 structure as a template. The ProteinPrepare tool from PlayMolecule package was used to estimate the protonation states for the histidines, especially those near ATP[50] . The respective crystal structures water molecules were transferred to the AlphaFoldmodeled structure of apo and the SWISS-MODEL-modeled structure of holo (i.e., waters from 5K3H were transferred to the modeled apo and waters from 5K3I were transferred to the modeled holo). For the apo 2A and 2B starting structures, the crystal waters from either subunit A or subunit B were duplicated. The characteristics of each system are summarized in Supplementary Table 1. 

The AMBER20 software suite was used for setting up and running the MD simulations[51] . FAD was parametrized with GAFF using the antechamber tool from AMBER[52] . The parameters for ATP were taken from the AMBER parameter database[53] .

The ff19SB force field was used for the enzyme with the OPC water model[54][,][55] . Minimization was carried out in six stages (4000 steps in each of them using the steepest descent algorithm for the first 2000 steps and using the conjugate gradient algorithm for the last 2000 steps while slowly decreasing the heavy atom restraints from 30 kcal/mol to 0[56][,][57] . Then the system was gradually heated to 298.15 K for 1 ns with a timestep of 1 fs under a constant volume condition. The heated system was then equilibrated with constant pressure (Berendsen thermostat[58] ) and temperature (Langevin thermostat[59] ), first for 1.1 ns with 5.0 kcal/ mol restraints on the heavy atoms (where first 0.1 ns were run on CPU and then moved to GPU for the next 1 ns), then for 5 ns without any restraints. For equilibration, we used timesteps of 1 fs, which is the same as we used in the heating stage. Afterward, all the equilibrated systems were simulated for production for 2 µs and then extended to 4 µs at 298.15 K with a constant pressure of 1 atm (Monte Carlo barostat) and constant temperature conditions (Langevin thermostat)[60] . Skin-permit parameter was set to 0.75 for better efficiency at the production stage without limiting the accuracy (https:// ambermd.org/GPULogistics.php), similar to as described[61] . At the production stage, we used hydrogen mass repartition and SHAKE constraints, allowing us to use a timestep of 4 fs[62][,][63] . A cutoff of 8 Å was used to approximate the long-range electrostatic interaction using the Particle–Mesh Ewald (PME) method[64] . Throughout the process, the collision frequency was set to 1 ps[−][1] . The production stage was run in 20 copies with unique “random numbers” for different copies to ensure the uniqueness of different copies.

## Clustering analysis 

For the ATP and FAD sites in the apo and holo MD simulations, we extracted the top 5% of frames with the largest opening distance and top 5% of frames with the smallest opening distance using the MDTraj package. Each subset of frames was clustered independently to identify a representative structure in each of those eight categories. We clustered each subset using the pairwise RMSD of the relevant ligand-binding sites as the similarity metric with the hierarchical agglomerative clustering algorithm implemented in cpptraj from the AMBER20 suite. In all cases, average linkage was used to calculate the distance between clusters with an RMSD cutoff of 1.5 Å. The ligand-binding site opening distances of the centroids for the top ten clusters in each category were calculated using the MDTraj package.

## Allosteric network analysis 

SenseNet (1.1.1) was used to calculate the allosteric network as a plugin of Cytoscape (3.10.1)[22][,][66] . For this purpose, two different time series were built using cpptraj tool from the AMBER20 suite, one for the hydrogen bond interaction network (with a 3.5 Å distance cutoff) and one for the heavy atom interaction network (with a 5 Å distance cutoff)[67] . For memory efficiency, we only used 500 equally spread-out frames from the first 10 (2 µs) MD simulations of the apo and holo enzymes for this analysis. After generating the time series, we used a JAVA (1.8.0_441) environment-dependent tool AIFgen (1.0.9) to convert the cpptraj output to the SenseNet-supported format AIF. The AIF file was loaded into SenseNet, ignoring the interactions that occur less than 50% of the time. Each residue in the enzyme was represented as a node, and the interactions between residues were represented as edges. First, the Edge Correlation Factor (ECF) was calculated using the “correlation” function using mutual information mode from the SenseNet GUI. This calculation resulted in correlation values for all residue pairs. The correlation values for each residue were summed up using the “Degree” function. These summed up correlation values for each residue were saved as allosteric correlation values. SenseNet allows us to estimate allosteric correlation in several different ways, such as Node Correlation Factor(NCF) and Difference Node Correlation Factor (DNCF). NCF is calculated fora single interaction system resulting from one system. Whereas the DNCF uses two interaction networks: one as a target network and another as a reference network.

In this work, we focused on the DNCF network as our goal is to understand the role of the cofactors (ATP and FAD in this case) in the system. Therefore, we used the interaction network from the holo system as the target and the interaction network of the apo system as the reference network. In Fig. 6a, residues with allosteric values in the top 10% were shown in the network for better visualization and the color was normalized from white-to-red for these residues based on theirraw allosteric correlation values. In Fig. 6b–d, allosteric values were normalized with z-score values, and graphically the network was visualized as white for nodes with negative z-score values and as a white-to-red gradient for positive z-score values. The most important path between two selected nodes was calculated by summing up the number of edges between pairs of residues.
